title: Conditionals
summary: Let your program pick which lines to run.
refresher: An `if` statement runs its body when the **condition** comes back true, and skips it otherwise. Java requires parentheses around that condition, and the braces `{ }` mark where the body starts and ends. Add `else if` for a second question, and `else` for the leftover case. Java tries the **branches** from the top and stops as soon as one of them fires. Use `==` on numbers, `&&` and `||` and `!` to combine conditions, and `.equals()` on **Strings**.

sections.title: The if statement shape
sections.summary: Use parentheses and braces so the branch body is clear.

blocks.body: A program that always runs the same lines in the same order can only ever do one thing. A **conditional** is how it starts reacting to what it was handed. You write a test that Java can settle as true or false, and the code attached to that test runs on true and is skipped on false.

blocks.caption: Before real syntax, learn the shape: ask a condition, then run only the matching **body**. The examples after this show the exact punctuation for this language.
blocks.code:
if condition is true:
    body for the true case
otherwise:
    body for the backup case

blocks.caption: Two pieces of punctuation carry the meaning here. The parentheses hold the **condition**, and Java requires them. The braces mark the body: everything between `{` and `}` runs only when the condition is true. The last line sits outside the braces, so it runs no matter what.

blocks.body: A Java program has a **class**, a `main` **method**, and statements inside that method. The examples below skip the wrapper so you can focus on the condition. Indentation helps humans read. Braces decide what Java runs.

blocks.title: A missing brace does not always break the program
blocks.body: Java allows an `if` with no braces when the body has one statement. Be careful: only the next statement belongs to the `if`. Lines after that run no matter what. Braces make your intent clear.

blocks.caption: Both versions compile. On the left, `temperature` is 40, so the "Hot" line never prints. Yet the shorts line prints anyway, because it was never inside the `if` to begin with. The braces on the right make the body explicit, and the code then does what it looks like it does.

blocks.body: Use braces every time, even for a one-line body. It costs you two characters and it removes a whole category of bug. Most teams and most professors require it for exactly that reason.

blocks.prompt: The programmer wanted nothing to **print** from the `if`, since `lives` is 0. What actually prints?
choices: Keep playing, then Score saved, then Game over
blocks.why: With no braces, the `if` owns exactly one statement: the "Keep playing" line. That is the only line it can skip, and `lives > 0` is false, so it is skipped. The "Score saved" line was never inside the `if`, no matter how far it is indented, so it runs. "Game over" runs too. If you picked "Game over only", you read the indentation the way a person would, and that is the trap: Java reads braces, and there are none here. Put braces around both lines and you get the behavior you wanted.

sections.title: Chains and assignment mistakes
sections.summary: Order else-if chains and avoid assignment where a comparison belongs.

blocks.body: Use `else if` when there is another test to try. Java reaches it only if the earlier test was false. Use `else` at the end for anything that did not match above.

blocks.caption: Java checks branches from top to bottom and stops at the first match. That means order matters. Put the most specific or highest-priority rule before a broader rule.

blocks.title: if (x = 5) will not compile
blocks.body: One `=` assigns a **value**. Two `==` compares values. `if (x = 5)` gives the `if` a number, but an `if` needs true or false. Java catches that before the program runs.
Java checks types while compiling. If the types do not fit, the program does not start. Read the file name and line number first.

sections.title: Combined conditions and text
sections.summary: Use logical operators and compare Strings by content.

blocks.body: You can join **conditions**. `&&` means both sides must be true. `||` means at least one side must be true. `!` flips true to false or false to true. Each side still needs a complete comparison, such as `age >= 13 && age <= 19`.

blocks.caption: Read joined conditions out loud. `age >= 13 && age <= 19` means both age checks must pass. `age < 5 || age >= 65` means either age check can pass. `!hasTicket` means "not has ticket."

blocks.title: Comparing Strings with == is the bug that hides
blocks.body: For **Strings**, use `.equals()` to compare text. `==` checks whether two names point to the same object, not whether the characters match. This is especially important for text from Scanner or a file.

blocks.caption: Both read a word typed by the user, and both compile. Type "yes" into each and only the right-hand version prints anything, because the typed **String** is a new **object** and `==` is asking the wrong question about it.

sections.title: Switch choices
sections.summary: Use switch carefully when one value chooses among fixed cases.

blocks.body: When one **value** is checked against several fixed possibilities, a `switch` says the same thing as a long `else if` chain with less repetition. Java compares the value against each `case` label and jumps to the one that matches. `default` runs when none of them do.

blocks.caption: Each `break` ends the switch. Leave one out and Java keeps running straight down into the cases below it, printing those too, which is almost never what you wanted. That behavior is called fall-through, and a missing `break` is the classic switch bug.

blocks.prompt: Every `break` has been left out of this switch. What does it **print**?
choices: Monday, Tuesday, and Some other day, on three lines
It does not compile, since every case needs a break
blocks.why: Java jumps to `case 1` because `day` is 1, and then it keeps going. A `case` label is a place to jump to, not a wall. With no `break` to stop it, execution falls straight through `case 2` and `default`, running all three prints. If you picked "Monday only", you read each case as a separate box, which is how an `else if` chain behaves but not a switch. And this compiles fine: a missing `break` is legal Java, so the compiler stays quiet while the program does the wrong thing. Put a `break` at the end of every case.

sections.title: Conditional habits
sections.summary: Use conditional rules before moving into practice.

blocks.title: Habits that keep Java conditionals honest
items: Wrap the **condition** in parentheses. Java will not compile `if x > 1` without them.
Use braces on every `if`, even a one-line body, so the body is never in doubt.
Order your **branches** from strictest to loosest, because whichever question fires first ends the chain.
Compare numbers with `==`, and compare **Strings** with `.equals()`.
End every `case` in a switch with a `break`, unless you actually want it to fall through.
Try the boundary **values**. For `score >= 90`, run 90 itself, then 89, then 91.
When the program does the wrong thing and reports no error at all, check the braces before you check anything else.

if-else-01.title: If and else choose one path
if-else-01.body: An if/else pair chooses between two alternatives. If the condition is true, the if body runs; otherwise the else body runs.
if-else-01.notice: Only one branch in the pair should run.
if-else-01.mistake: Do not expect the else branch to run after a true if branch.

chain-first-true-01.title: A chain stops at the first true branch
chain-first-true-01.body: In an if/else-if chain, the program checks from top to bottom and runs the first branch whose condition is true.
chain-first-true-01.notice: Later branches are skipped once an earlier branch wins.
chain-first-true-01.mistake: Do not choose a later true branch when an earlier true branch already matched.

separate-ifs-01.title: Separate if statements are independent
separate-ifs-01.body: Two separate if statements each ask their own question. Both can run if both conditions are true.
separate-ifs-01.notice: Separate if statements are not alternatives unless they are connected with else-if or else.
separate-ifs-01.mistake: Do not treat separate ifs like a single chain.

assign-vs-compare-01.title: Conditions compare, assignments store
assign-vs-compare-01.body: A condition should produce true or false. Use comparison when asking whether a value matches something.
assign-vs-compare-01.notice: Assignment and comparison are different jobs.
assign-vs-compare-01.mistake: Do not use assignment syntax when the condition should be a yes/no test.

and-or-01.title: And means both; or means either
and-or-01.body: Use and when every rule must be true. Use or when one matching rule is enough.
and-or-01.notice: Try a value outside the range to test whether the condition is too loose.
and-or-01.mistake: Do not use or for a between rule unless either side really should pass.

body-scope-01.title: Only the branch body is controlled
body-scope-01.body: A conditional controls the statements inside its body. Code after the branch runs normally unless another condition stops it.
body-scope-01.notice: Indentation or braces decide what belongs to the branch.
body-scope-01.mistake: Do not assume every line nearby is controlled by the if.

chain-order-01.title: Order matters in condition chains
chain-order-01.body: Put the most specific or highest-priority condition before a broader one when only one branch should run.
chain-order-01.notice: A broad condition can catch a value before a later, more specific condition gets a chance.
chain-order-01.mistake: Do not place a general true condition above the branch you actually wanted.

not-operator-01.title: Not flips a condition
not-operator-01.body: The not operator changes true to false and false to true. It is useful when the branch should run for the opposite case.
not-operator-01.notice: Read the condition slowly with the word not included.
not-operator-01.mistake: Do not ignore not when predicting which branch runs.

nested-if-01.title: Nested conditions need the outer branch first
nested-if-01.body: An inner if is checked only after the outer if lets the program enter that block.
nested-if-01.notice: Trace the outer condition before deciding whether the inner one matters.
nested-if-01.mistake: Do not jump to the inner branch when the outer condition is false.

boundary-01.title: Boundaries decide edge cases
boundary-01.body: When a rule mentions values at the edge, check whether the comparison includes or excludes that exact value.
boundary-01.notice: `>=` and `<=` include the boundary. `>` and `<` exclude it.
boundary-01.mistake: Do not test only middle values; edge values reveal boundary mistakes.
